blocks.text: Above all I like the acumen of Thomas, who, following the version and order of Jerome, transfers something from each of these birds to morals. "In the eagle," he says ^{c)}, "which flies high, pride is forbidden. In the gryphon, which is hostile to horses and men, the cruelty of the powerful is forbidden. In the haliaeetus, which feeds on small birds, those are signified who harass the poor. In the kite, which makes the greatest use of ambushes, the deceitful are signified. In the vulture, which follows an army, waiting to eat the corpses of the dead, those are signified who strive after the deaths and seditions of men, so as to profit from them." Read the passage, and you will see that he pursues the rest with equal care. Yet he does so in such a way that he reports certain things about the birds that are not quite true: 1. for instance, that the porphyrio has one foot broad for swimming and the other split for walking; that the herodio (that is, the ardea [heron]) is the same as the falcon; that the caladrius (that is, the charadrius) is a garrulous bird, etc. He also has some ἀποδόσεις [apodoseis] that are forced and extorted by violence, which was the malady of those times. Nevertheless, in many places the talent of that man shines forth, worthy of a better age.
